claim: Production of most eukaryotic mRNAs requires splicing of introns from pre-mRNA.
source: Production of most eukaryotic mRNAs requires splicing of introns from pre-mRNA.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in molecular biology supported by scientific consensus.

claim: The splicing reaction requires definition of splice sites, which are initially recognized in either intron-spanning ('intron definition') or exon-spanning ('exon definition') pairs.
source: The splicing reaction requires definition of splice sites, which are initially recognized in either intron-spanning ('intron definition') or exon-spanning ('exon definition') pairs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about splice site recognition modes in the field.

claim: The modal intron length range of 60–70 nt represents a local maximum of splicing rates in Drosophila.
source: We found that the modal intron length range of 60–70 nt represents a local maximum of splicing rates, but that much longer exon-defined introns are spliced even faster and more accurately.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements of splicing rates across different intron lengths shown in the manuscript.

claim: Much longer exon-defined introns are spliced even faster and more accurately than 60-70 nt introns.
source: We found that the modal intron length range of 60–70 nt represents a local maximum of splicing rates, but that much longer exon-defined introns are spliced even faster and more accurately.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing splicing rates and accuracy across different intron length classes.

claim: There is unexpectedly low variation in splicing rates across introns in the same gene.
source: We observed unexpectedly low variation in splicing rates across introns in the same gene, suggesting the presence of gene-level influences, and we identified multiple gene level variables associated with splicing rate.
evidence: This observation is based on analysis of splicing rate data across multiple introns within genes.

claim: Multiple gene level variables are associated with splicing rate.
source: We observed unexpectedly low variation in splicing rates across introns in the same gene, suggesting the presence of gene-level influences, and we identified multiple gene level variables associated with splicing rate.
evidence: This is supported by regression analysis identifying gene-level features that correlate with splicing rates.

claim: Developmental and stress response genes may have preferentially evolved exon definition in order to enhance the rate or accuracy of splicing.
source: Together our data suggest that developmental and stress response genes may have preferentially evolved exon definition in order to enhance the rate or accuracy of splicing.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed enrichment of exon-defined introns in developmental and stress response genes and their faster/more accurate splicing.

claim: Average intron lengths exceed 1 or 2 kilobases in most vertebrates compared to 50–500 nt in simpler eukaryotes.
source: For example, average intron lengths exceed 1 or 2 kilobases in most vertebrates compared to 50–500 nt in simpler eukaryotes, with somewhat less variability in exon lengths (Deutsch and Long, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: There is somewhat less variability in exon lengths across organisms than in intron lengths.
source: For example, average intron lengths exceed 1 or 2 kilobases in most vertebrates compared to 50–500 nt in simpler eukaryotes, with somewhat less variability in exon lengths (Deutsch and Long, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The presence and density of introns can influence gene expression levels.
source: The presence and density of introns can influence gene expression levels (Mascarenhas et al., 1990; Chung et al., 2006; Shaul, 2017), while longer flanking intron lengths are associated with alternatively spliced exons (Fox-Walsh et al., 2005; Gelfman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Longer flanking intron lengths are associated with alternatively spliced exons.
source: The presence and density of introns can influence gene expression levels (Mascarenhas et al., 1990; Chung et al., 2006; Shaul, 2017), while longer flanking intron lengths are associated with alternatively spliced exons (Fox-Walsh et al., 2005; Gelfman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The splicing of metazoan introns requires three primary sequence elements: the 5' splice site, the 3' splice site and polypyrimidine tract, and the branch point sequence.
source: The splicing of metazoan introns requires three primary sequence elements – the 5' splice site (at the exon/intron boundary), the 3' splice site and polypyrimidine tract (at and upstream of the intron/exon boundary), and the branch point sequence (BPS) – and the numerous (ribonucleo)proteins that make up the spliceosome.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the molecular requirements for splicing.

claim: The earliest steps in splicing are the base pairing of the U1 and U2 small ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs) to the 5' splice site and BPS, respectively.
source: The earliest steps in splicing are the base pairing of the U1 and U2 small ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs) to the 5' splice site and BPS, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of splicing.

claim: In intron definition, the U1 and U2 snRNPs first interact across the intron.
source: Progression toward splicing is thought to occur in one of two modes – either by 'intron definition,' in which the U1 and U2 snRNPs first interact across the intron; or 'exon definition,' in which U1 snRNP initially pairs with the upstream U2 snRNP across the exon, followed by rearrangement to form interactions with the downstream U2 snRNP across the intron (Berget, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: In exon definition, U1 snRNP initially pairs with the upstream U2 snRNP across the exon, followed by rearrangement to form interactions with the downstream U2 snRNP across the intron.
source: Progression toward splicing is thought to occur in one of two modes – either by 'intron definition,' in which the U1 and U2 snRNPs first interact across the intron; or 'exon definition,' in which U1 snRNP initially pairs with the upstream U2 snRNP across the exon, followed by rearrangement to form interactions with the downstream U2 snRNP across the intron (Berget, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Intron splicing is likely the rate-limiting step in the production of many processed mRNAs.
source: Although intron splicing is likely the rate-limiting step in the production of many processed mRNAs, the precise mechanisms and consequences of differing splice-site recognition modes remains unclear.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetics of gene expression steps.

claim: The architecture of a gene – specifically the absolute or relative lengths of introns and exons – is important for the selection of a splice-site recognition mode.
source: Previous observations suggest that the architecture of a gene – specifically the absolute or relative lengths of introns and exons (Robberson et al., 1990; Sterner et al., 1996; Berget, 1995) – is important for the selection of a splice-site recognition mode, with the shorter sized unit being favored for initial pairing of snRNPs (Talerico and Berget, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: The shorter sized unit is favored for initial pairing of snRNPs.
source: Previous observations suggest that the architecture of a gene – specifically the absolute or relative lengths of introns and exons (Robberson et al., 1990; Sterner et al., 1996; Berget, 1995) – is important for the selection of a splice-site recognition mode, with the shorter sized unit being favored for initial pairing of snRNPs (Talerico and Berget, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: In vertebrate genomes, exon definition is thought to be the predominant recognition mode.
source: In vertebrate genomes, where exon definition is thought to be the predominant recognition mode, the experimental expansion of exon lengths can prevent proper spliceosome formation (Sterner et al., 1996) except when the flanking introns are very short (Chen and Chasin, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The experimental expansion of exon lengths can prevent proper spliceosome formation in vertebrate genomes except when the flanking introns are very short.
source: In vertebrate genomes, where exon definition is thought to be the predominant recognition mode, the experimental expansion of exon lengths can prevent proper spliceosome formation (Sterner et al., 1996) except when the flanking introns are very short (Chen and Chasin, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: In yeast and Drosophila, the expansion of small introns can lead to intron retention and other splicing defects.
source: In yeast and Drosophila, the expansion of small introns can lead to intron retention and other splicing defects (Guo et al., 1993; Talerico and Berget, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Recognition of introns and exons larger than 300–500 nt can be inefficient, unless the flanking units are much smaller.
source: Some studies have suggested that recognition of introns and exons larger than 300–500 nt can be inefficient, unless the flanking units are much smaller (Fox-Walsh et al., 2005; Sterner et al., 1996; Chen and Chasin, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: There is a minimum 5' splice site to branch point distance in each organism, which imposes a minimal intronic length.
source: There is also a minimum 5' splice site to branch point distance in each organism, which imposes a minimal intronic length, and splicing of very small exons is generally inefficient due to steric interference between bound factors (Dominski and Kole, 1991; Black, 1991; Sterner et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Splicing of very small exons is generally inefficient due to steric interference between bound factors.
source: There is also a minimum 5' splice site to branch point distance in each organism, which imposes a minimal intronic length, and splicing of very small exons is generally inefficient due to steric interference between bound factors (Dominski and Kole, 1991; Black, 1991; Sterner et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: For shorter intron-defined introns, intron length might limit the rate of diffusion-based contact between the U1 and U2 snRNPs.
source: For shorter intron-defined introns, intron length might limit the rate of diffusion-based contact between the U1 and U2 snRNPs (Hollander et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: For longer exon-defined introns which must undergo two recognition steps, a passive diffusion-based model would predict prohibitively slow splicing rates.
source: However, for longer exon-defined introns which must undergo two recognition steps, this passive diffusion-based model would predict prohibitively slow splicing rates (Hollander et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on a model described in cited literature.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster has a broad distribution of intron lengths, with over a third of introns between 60 and 70 nt, and a tail of longer introns with lengths up to tens of kilobases.
source: Furthermore, Drosophila melanogaster has a broad distribution of intron lengths (Lim and Burge, 2001), with over a third of introns between 60 and 70 nt, and a tail of longer introns with lengths up to tens of kilobases (kb).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Splicing is thought to predominantly occur co-transcriptionally.
source: Splicing is thought to predominantly occur co-transcriptionally (Singh and Padgett, 2009; Khodor et al., 2011; Schmidt et al., 2011; Brugiolo et al., 2013), with measured rates for a handful of mammalian introns of 0.5–10 min (Singh and Padgett, 2009; Schmidt et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2013; Rabani et al., 2014) while yeast introns are often spliced within seconds after synthesis (Eser et al., 2016; Oesterreich et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Measured rates for a handful of mammalian introns are 0.5–10 min.
source: Splicing is thought to predominantly occur co-transcriptionally (Singh and Padgett, 2009; Khodor et al., 2011; Schmidt et al., 2011; Brugiolo et al., 2013), with measured rates for a handful of mammalian introns of 0.5–10 min (Singh and Padgett, 2009; Schmidt et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2013; Rabani et al., 2014) while yeast introns are often spliced within seconds after synthesis (Eser et al., 2016; Oesterreich et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Yeast introns are often spliced within seconds after synthesis.
source: Splicing is thought to predominantly occur co-transcriptionally (Singh and Padgett, 2009; Khodor et al., 2011; Schmidt et al., 2011; Brugiolo et al., 2013), with measured rates for a handful of mammalian introns of 0.5–10 min (Singh and Padgett, 2009; Schmidt et al., 2011; Martin et al., 2013; Rabani et al., 2014) while yeast introns are often spliced within seconds after synthesis (Eser et al., 2016; Oesterreich et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The splicing of U12-type introns can be rate-limiting, such that splicing can be made more efficient by mutating U12-type splice sites to sites recognized by the major U2-type spliceosome in Drosophila cells.
source: For instance, the splicing of U12-type introns (spliced by the minor spliceosome) can be rate-limiting, such that splicing – and the ultimate production of mature mRNAs – can be made more efficient by mutating U12-type splice sites to sites recognized by the major U2-type spliceosome in Drosophila cells (Singh and Padgett, 2009; Patel et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Alternatively spliced introns are spliced at different rates than constitutive introns.
source: Previous studies have suggested that alternatively spliced introns are spliced at different rates than constitutive introns (Fong et al., 2014; Kwak et al., 2013; Jonkers et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The junction dynamics approach was best able to accurately order introns by rate and assign absolute rates to each intron in simulations.
source: Overall, the junction dynamics approach was best able to accurately order introns by rate, and also accurately assign absolute rates to each intron in our simulations.
evidence: This is based on simulation results comparing different methods.

claim: The Ψ decrease and junction dynamics approaches both yielded rankings of half-lives very similar to those used in the simulation (rSpearman = 0.99 and 0.95, respectively).
source: Considering relative orderings, the Ψ decrease and junction dynamics approaches both yielded rankings of half-lives very similar to those used in the simulation (rSpearman = 0.99 and 0.95, respectively), while the intron ratio approach correlated more weakly (rSpearman = 0.57; Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), indicating much poorer agreement.
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in figures.

claim: The intron ratio approach correlated more weakly (rSpearman = 0.57) with simulated half-lives than other approaches.
source: Considering relative orderings, the Ψ decrease and junction dynamics approaches both yielded rankings of half-lives very similar to those used in the simulation (rSpearman = 0.99 and 0.95, respectively), while the intron ratio approach correlated more weakly (rSpearman = 0.57; Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), indicating much poorer agreement.
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in figures.

claim: Half-lives estimated by the junction dynamics approach differed by just 21% on average from the simulated values.
source: Assessing absolute estimation of half-lives, we found that half-lives estimated by the junction dynamics approach differed by just 21% on average from the simulated values, while the Ψ decrease approach tended to overestimate half-lives substantially (Figure 1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in figures.

claim: The Ψ decrease approach tended to overestimate half-lives substantially.
source: Assessing absolute estimation of half-lives, we found that half-lives estimated by the junction dynamics approach differed by just 21% on average from the simulated values, while the Ψ decrease approach tended to overestimate half-lives substantially (Figure 1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in figures.

claim: The junction dynamics method accurately recovered half-lives across the full range of simulated values (rPearson = 0.95), with no detectible bias.
source: The junction dynamics method accurately recovered half-lives across the full range of simulated values (rPearson = 0.95), with no detectible bias, while the Ψ decrease method consistently overestimates absolute half-lives, with greater absolute deviation from true values at longer half-lives (rPearson = 0.35; Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in figures.

claim: The Ψ decrease method consistently overestimates absolute half-lives, with greater absolute deviation from true values at longer half-lives (rPearson = 0.35).
source: The junction dynamics method accurately recovered half-lives across the full range of simulated values (rPearson = 0.95), with no detectible bias, while the Ψ decrease method consistently overestimates absolute half-lives, with greater absolute deviation from true values at longer half-lives (rPearson = 0.35; Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in figures.

claim: The experimental approach involved 5, 10, and 20 min labeling with 4-thiouridine (4sU), followed by RNA sequencing of three replicates per labeling period.
source: Our experimental approach involved 5, 10, and 20 min labeling with 4-thiouridine (4sU), followed by RNA sequencing of three replicates per labeling period.
evidence: This describes the experimental design used in the study.

claim: Intron half-lives were obtained for 25,576 constitutive introns in 5608 Drosophila genes with sufficient expression in S2 cells.
source: Applying our junction dynamics method, as described above, we obtained intron half-lives with associated confidence intervals and goodness-of-fit statistics for 25,576 constitutive introns in 5608 Drosophila genes with sufficient expression in S2 cells (Materials and methods, representative examples in Figure 1G–H; Figure 1—figure supplement 3C–D; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the results of applying the method to experimental data.

claim: The median intron half-life (t1/2) was 2.0 min.
source: The median intron half-life (t1/2) was 2.0 min, with most half-lives estimated here lying between those previously estimated in yeast (seconds) and mammalian cells (30 s to 10 min) using qRT-PCR or imaging approaches (Oesterreich et al., 2016; Eser et al., 2016; Singh and Padgett, 2009; Martin et al., 2013; Coulon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experimental data.

claim: For typical Drosophila genes of 3–9 kb in length, the estimated time of transcription is about 2–6 min.
source: For typical Drosophila genes of 3–9 kb in length, the estimated time of transcription is about 2–6 min (Ardehali and Lis, 2009).
evidence: This is based on citation to published literature.

claim: The estimated median intron half-life of ~2 min is consistent with splicing occurring co-transcriptionally for the majority of fly introns.
source: Thus, our estimated median intron half-life of ~2 min is consistent with splicing occurring co-transcriptionally for the majority of fly introns (Khodor et al., 2011; Brugiolo et al., 2013; Braunschweig et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing measured half-lives to transcription times, supported by citations.

claim: Estimated half-lives are robust with respect to transcription rate, varying by only ~10% on average for transcription rates between 1 and 3 kb/min.
source: Our approach assumes an average transcription rate across the gene body of 1.5 kb/min (Ardehali and Lis, 2009; Garcia et al., 2013). Estimated half-lives are robust with respect to this parameter, varying by only ~10% on average for transcription rates between 1 and 3 kb/min (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is based on sensitivity analysis shown in a figure.

claim: There was an overall weak positive relationship between intron lengths and estimated splicing half-lives across the entire distribution (rSpearman = 0.1, p-value<2.2×10−16).
source: While there was an overall weak positive relationship between intron lengths and estimated splicing half-lives across the entire distribution (rSpearman = 0.1, p-value<2.2×10−16), a notable decrease in half-life occurred near the short end of the intron length distribution (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Introns with lengths in the range 60–70 nt were spliced most rapidly (median t½=1.7 min).
source: Examining the rates for different bins of intron length in this vicinity, we found that introns with lengths in the range 60–70 nt were spliced most rapidly (median t½=1.7 min, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Median t½ increased steadily to 2.2 min for introns > 80 nt.
source: Median t½ increased steadily to 2.2 min for introns > 80 nt, and was also substantially higher for 'ultra-short' introns between 40–50 nt (median t1/2 of 2.7 min).
evidence: This is based on analysis of experimental data.

claim: Ultra-short introns between 40–50 nt had a median t1/2 of 2.7 min.
source: Median t½ increased steadily to 2.2 min for introns > 80 nt, and was also substantially higher for 'ultra-short' introns between 40–50 nt (median t1/2 of 2.7 min).
evidence: This is based on analysis of experimental data.

claim: Ultra-short introns had substantially weaker 3' splice site scores than other introns.
source: These ultra-short introns had substantially weaker 3' splice site scores than other introns (Farlow et al., 2012) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), and 60–70 nt introns with similarly weak 3' splice sites were spliced at similar rates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that 3' splice site weakness is a cause of slower splicing.
evidence: This is based on analysis of splice site scores shown in figures.

claim: 60–70 nt introns with similarly weak 3' splice sites were spliced at similar rates to ultra-short introns, suggesting that 3' splice site weakness is a cause of slower splicing.
source: These ultra-short introns had substantially weaker 3' splice site scores than other introns (Farlow et al., 2012) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), and 60–70 nt introns with similarly weak 3' splice sites were spliced at similar rates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that 3' splice site weakness is a cause of slower splicing.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing splicing rates of introns with matched splice site strengths.

claim: The mean location of the BPS motif was much closer to the 3'ss in ultra-short introns (–14) than in the longer intron classes, where the mean location was between –23 and –26.
source: However, the mean location of this motif was much closer to the 3'ss in ultra-short introns (–14) than in the longer intron classes, where the mean location was between –23 and –26.
evidence: This is based on analysis of branch point sequence positions.

claim: Ultra-short introns are constrained in their ability to splice efficiently by their suboptimal BPS locations.
source: This observation suggests that ultra-short introns are constrained in their ability to splice efficiently by their suboptimal BPS locations, which may simply prevent a sufficiently long PPT for efficient splicing, or may result in steric interference between dU2AF50 bound at the PPT and U2 snRNP bound at the BPS (Black, 1991; De Conti et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed BPS positions and known mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: Natural selection favors short intron lengths in Drosophila.
source: These observations, in conjunction with evidence that natural selection favors short intron lengths in Drosophila (Carvalho and Clark, 1999; Parsch, 2003; Parsch et al., 2010), suggests that selection on intron lengths for efficient splicing contributes to the observed peak of intron size near ~65 nt.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Selection on intron lengths for efficient splicing contributes to the observed peak of intron size near ~65 nt.
source: These observations, in conjunction with evidence that natural selection favors short intron lengths in Drosophila (Carvalho and Clark, 1999; Parsch, 2003; Parsch et al., 2010), suggests that selection on intron lengths for efficient splicing contributes to the observed peak of intron size near ~65 nt.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed relationship between intron length and splicing rate, combined with evidence of selection.

claim: Alternatively retained introns that are constitutively spliced out in S2 cells have significantly slower splicing half-lives than constitutive introns, independent of intron length.
source: We observed that such RIs have significantly slower splicing half-lives than constitutive introns (CI), independent of intron length, as do introns that flank exons alternatively skipped in other cells/tissues (SEflanking) (all Mann-Whitney p<0.01 for all comparisons between CI and RI and between CI and SEflanking; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Introns that flank exons alternatively skipped in other cells/tissues have significantly slower splicing half-lives than constitutive introns.
source: We observed that such RIs have significantly slower splicing half-lives than constitutive introns (CI), independent of intron length, as do introns that flank exons alternatively skipped in other cells/tissues (SEflanking) (all Mann-Whitney p<0.01 for all comparisons between CI and RI and between CI and SEflanking; Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: The capacity for splicing regulation may impose limits on the rates of intron splicing.
source: This observation suggests that the capacity for splicing regulation may impose limits on the rates of intron splicing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that alternatively spliced introns are spliced more slowly.

claim: Introns that are shorter than the mean length of their flanking exons (RIME <1) are more likely to undergo intron definition.
source: Based on the consensus noted above, introns that are shorter than the mean length of their flanking exons (RIME <1) are more likely to undergo intron definition, while introns with RIME values > 1 may favor exon definition.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about splice site recognition modes.

claim: Introns with RIME values > 1 may favor exon definition.
source: Based on the consensus noted above, introns that are shorter than the mean length of their flanking exons (RIME <1) are more likely to undergo intron definition, while introns with RIME values > 1 may favor exon definition.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about splice site recognition modes.

claim: Introns with RIME near one tended to have longer splicing half-lives.
source: Also notable was a horizontal yellow stripe representing long introns with the highest RIME values, while introns with RIME near one tended to have longer splicing half-lives (Figure 3D–E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Length combinations more predictive of exon definition (RIME > 1) or intron definition (RIME < 1) were spliced more rapidly, while intermediate combinations with ambiguous splicing mode were associated with slower splicing.
source: This pattern is consistent with the idea that length combinations more predictive of exon definition (RIME > 1) or intron definition (RIME < 1) were spliced more rapidly, while intermediate combinations with ambiguous splicing mode were associated with slower splicing (see Discussion).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed pattern of splicing rates across RIME values.

claim: For introns likely to undergo intron definition (RIME <<1), the longest intron lengths (>99 nt) were associated with the slowest splicing.
source: For introns likely to undergo intron definition (RIME <<1), the longest intron lengths (>99 nt) were associated with the slowest splicing.
evidence: This is based on analysis of experimental data.

claim: For introns likely to undergo exon definition, the longest intron lengths (>2944 nt) were associated with the fastest splicing rates.
source: In contrast, for introns likely to undergo exon definition, the longest intron lengths (>2944 nt) were associated with the fastest splicing rates (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is based on analysis of experimental data shown in a figure.

claim: Exon and intron definition modes may have fundamentally different kinetics, perhaps with different rate-limiting steps.
source: This surprising observation suggests that exon and intron definition modes may have fundamentally different kinetics, perhaps with different rate-limiting steps (see Discussion).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences in how intron length affects splicing rate in different recognition modes.

claim: Putatively exon-defined introns (high RIME) had an abundance of significantly enriched 6mers in the flanking exons but no significant 6mers in intronic regions.
source: Strikingly, putatively exon-defined introns (high RIME) had an abundance of significantly enriched 6mers in the flanking exons but no significant 6mers in intronic regions (Figure 3G; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of sequence motif enrichment shown in figures.

claim: Low RIME introns had many significant 6mers in intronic regions, and relatively few in the flanking exons.
source: In contrast, low RIME introns had many significant 6mers in intronic regions, and relatively few in the flanking exons.
evidence: This is based on analysis of sequence motif enrichment.

claim: The overall asymmetry in 6mer enrichment supports a role for region-specific sequence features in splice-site recognition modes.
source: The overall asymmetry in 6mer enrichment supports a role for region-specific sequence features in splice-site recognition modes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed pattern of motif enrichment.

claim: AACAAC, CAACAA, and ACAACA were among the top enriched 6mers in both upstream and downstream exons flanking exon-defined introns.
source: For example, AACAAC, CAACAA, and ACAACA, among the top enriched 6mers in both upstream and downstream exons flanking exon-defined introns, were among the five most enriched 6mers in exons flanking alternative exons regulated in S2 cells by the Drosophila splicing factor Pasilla (PS), a homolog of mammalian Nova family splicing factors which bind a distinct but related motif, YCAY (Brooks et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on analysis of motif enrichment and comparison to known binding motifs, supported by citation.

claim: The most enriched 6mer in downstream exons, GCAGCA, is a known mammalian exonic splicing enhancer and a binding motif for the SR proteins SRSF8 and SRSF10.
source: The most enriched 6mer in downstream exons, GCAGCA, is a known mammalian exonic splicing enhancer (Fairbrother et al., 2002) and a binding motif for the SR proteins SRSF8 and SRSF10 (Dominguez et al.).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Longer exon-defined introns are preceded by upstream exons with a higher density of significant 6mers than shorter exon-defined introns.
source: Indeed, longer exon-defined introns – which are spliced more quickly – are preceded by upstream exons with a higher density of significant 6mers (in aggregate) than shorter exon-defined introns (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of motif density shown in a figure.

claim: Exon-defined introns (high RIME) had the lowest mean frequency of non-canonical junction reads.
source: Despite being longer, exon-defined introns (high RIME) had the lowest mean frequency of non-canonical junction reads, while intron-defined introns (low RIME) had highest frequency of non-canonical splice site usage (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is based on analysis of splicing accuracy shown in a figure.

claim: Intron-defined introns (low RIME) had highest frequency of non-canonical splice site usage.
source: Despite being longer, exon-defined introns (high RIME) had the lowest mean frequency of non-canonical junction reads, while intron-defined introns (low RIME) had highest frequency of non-canonical splice site usage (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is based on analysis of splicing accuracy shown in a figure.

claim: The initial recognition of splice sites across exon units involved in exon definition may improve the accuracy of splice site choice.
source: This observation suggests that the initial recognition of splice sites across exon units involved in exon definition may improve the accuracy of splice site choice.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed lower error rates in exon-defined introns.

claim: Intron length was one of the strongest contributors to variance in splicing rates for both intron- and exon-defined introns.
source: Intron length was one of the strongest contributors for both sets of introns, contributing positively to splicing rate for the exon-defined class and negatively for the intron-defined class, consistent with results shown in Figure 3E.
evidence: This is based on multiple linear regression analysis of the data.

claim: Intron length contributes positively to splicing rate for the exon-defined class and negatively for the intron-defined class.
source: Intron length was one of the strongest contributors for both sets of introns, contributing positively to splicing rate for the exon-defined class and negatively for the intron-defined class, consistent with results shown in Figure 3E.
evidence: This is based on multiple linear regression analysis of the data.

claim: Increased strength of both the 5' and 3' splice sites was associated with shorter intron half-lives.
source: As expected, increased strength of both the 5' and 3' splice sites was associated with shorter intron half-lives (Hicks et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on regression analysis and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: 5' splice site strength appeared more important for intron-defined introns, while 3' splice site strength had a greater impact for exon-defined introns.
source: However, 5' splice site strength appeared more important for intron-defined introns, while 3' splice site strength had a greater impact for exon-defined introns, consistent with models of splice site recognition (De Conti et al., 2013; Hollander et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on regression analysis and is consistent with cited models.

claim: A + U content of the intron was associated with shorter intron half-lives, especially in the 3' region of the intron.
source: A + U content of the intron was also associated with shorter intron half-lives, especially in the 3' region of the intron (excluding the 3' splice site).
evidence: This is based on regression analysis of the data.

claim: Gene expression level was one of the features most strongly associated with faster splicing in both splice site recognition modes.
source: One of the features most strongly associated with faster splicing in both splice site recognition modes was gene expression level, a property of the gene rather than of the intron.
evidence: This is based on regression analysis of the data.

claim: More rapidly spliced introns, particularly exon-defined introns, tend to occur in higher expressed genes.
source: This relationship is consistent with our observation that more rapidly spliced introns, particularly exon-defined introns, tend to occur in higher expressed genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the relationship between splicing rate and gene expression shown in a figure.

claim: Greater first intron length was associated with faster splicing of other introns for the intron definition class.
source: Greater first intron length was also associated with faster splicing of other introns for the intron definition class.
evidence: This is based on regression analysis of the data.

claim: Splicing half-lives of introns drawn from the same gene tend to be more similar to each other than those of randomly sampled introns.
source: We observed that splicing half-lives of introns drawn from the same gene tend to be more similar to each other (than those of randomly sampled introns, for example, comparing standard deviations (Mann-Whitney comparison of SDs, p<2.2 × 10−16; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the data shown in a figure.

claim: Introns from the same gene are more likely to have similar lengths than randomly sampled introns.
source: Introns from the same gene are also more likely to have similar lengths than randomly sampled introns (Mann-Whitney comparison of SDs, p<2.2 × 10−16, Figure 4C), suggesting that there might be an advantage to maintaining a consistent splice site recognition mode across introns within a gene.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the data shown in a figure.

claim: There might be an advantage to maintaining a consistent splice site recognition mode across introns within a gene.
source: Introns from the same gene are also more likely to have similar lengths than randomly sampled introns (Mann-Whitney comparison of SDs, p<2.2 × 10−16, Figure 4C), suggesting that there might be an advantage to maintaining a consistent splice site recognition mode across introns within a gene.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed similarity in intron lengths within genes.

claim: Splicing half-lives of introns drawn from genes with consistent splice site pairing preferences tend to be more similar to each other than introns from mixed definition genes.
source: We observed that splicing half-lives of introns drawn from genes with consistent splice site pairing preferences (classes 1 and 2) tend to be more similar to each other than introns from mixed definition genes.
evidence: This is based on analysis of variance in splicing rates across different gene classes.

claim: Splicing half-lives across introns from genes with mostly exon-defined introns were less than half as variable than half-lives across introns from intron-defined genes.
source: Notably, splicing half-lives across introns from genes with mostly exon-defined introns were less than half as variable than half-lives across introns from intron-defined genes (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of variance shown in a figure.

claim: First introns are more than twice as long on average as other introns in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, first introns are more than twice as long on average as other introns (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A) and take at least 50% longer to splice than second, third, fourth, or other intron positions.
evidence: This is based on analysis of intron lengths and splicing rates shown in a figure.

claim: First introns take at least 50% longer to splice than second, third, fourth, or other intron positions.
source: In Drosophila, first introns are more than twice as long on average as other introns (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A) and take at least 50% longer to splice than second, third, fourth, or other intron positions.
evidence: This is based on analysis of splicing rates shown in a figure.

claim: In metazoans, transcriptional enhancers are often located in the first introns of genes.
source: In metazoans, transcriptional enhancers are often located in the first introns of genes (Kharchenko et al., 2011; Arnold et al., 2013), and we confirmed this trend in genes expressed in S2 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by citations and confirmed by analysis shown in a figure.

claim: Presence of a transcriptional enhancer in any intron was associated with slower splicing of intron-defined introns and faster splicing of exon-defined introns.
source: Presence of a transcriptional enhancer in any intron (first and non-first) was associated with slower splicing of intron-defined introns and faster splicing of exon-defined introns (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C), but this association was not significant for introns from either splice site recognition mode in the regression model of splicing rates including other variables described above, so was not further explored here.
evidence: This is based on analysis shown in a figure, though the association was not significant in multivariate analysis.

claim: There is a weak but significant negative correlation between the length of the first intron in a gene and the median half-lives across downstream introns (rspearman = −0.06; p=0.00034).
source: We observed a weak but significant negative correlation between the length of the first intron in a gene and the median half-lives across downstream introns (rspearman = −0.06; p=0.00034; Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the data shown in a figure.

claim: The architecture of the 5' end of the gene, notably the length of the 5'-most intron, impacts the splicing efficiency of the remaining introns.
source: These observations suggest that the architecture of the 5' end of the gene, notably the length of the 5'-most intron, impacts the splicing efficiency of the remaining introns.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed correlation between first intron length and downstream intron splicing rates.

claim: Various properties of the gene – including its overall exon-intron architecture – impact the splicing rate of all introns, rather than each intron's splicing rate being independently determined.
source: These observations, together with our results in Figure 4A and B, suggest that various properties of the gene – including its overall exon-intron architecture – impact the splicing rate of all introns, rather than each intron's splicing rate being independently determined.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple observations about gene-level effects on splicing rates.

claim: Longer first introns might allow additional time for the recruitment of factors that promote downstream splicing efficiency.
source: Longer first introns might allow additional time for the recruitment of factors that promote downstream splicing efficiency, consistent with the observation that transcription elongation is slow before reaching the second exon, at least in mammalian cells (Jonkers and Lis, 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Under a model where longer first introns allow time for factor recruitment, longer first introns should be favored in genes with larger numbers of introns.
source: Under this model, longer first introns should be favored in genes with larger numbers of introns, where the splicing time of the first intron is less likely to be rate-limiting, because of the longer time required for the polymerase to reach the 3' end of the transcript and the greater likelihood that another intron's splicing is rate-limiting for production of mature mRNA.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the proposed model.

claim: Genes with larger numbers of introns have longer first introns.
source: Consistent with this expectation, we observed a pronounced trend where genes with larger numbers of introns have longer first introns (Figure 4—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is based on analysis of data shown in a figure.

claim: There is a well-established mutational bias toward short deletions (over short insertions) in the Drosophila lineage.
source: There is a well-established mutational bias toward short deletions (over short insertions) in the Drosophila lineage (Petrov et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The mutational bias toward deletions may explain the predominance of short introns in the D. melanogaster genome.
source: This bias may explain the predominance of short introns in the D. melanogaster genome (Comeron and Kreitman, 2000; Parsch, 2003; Lim and Burge, 2001).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The peak in intron length distribution at 60-70 nt may have been shaped by selection for efficient splicing.
source: Our observation that the 60–70 nt length range – where there is a sharp peak in the genome-wide intron length distribution – represents a local maximum in intron splicing rates, suggests that this peak may have been shaped by selection for efficient splicing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed relationship between intron length and splicing rate.

claim: At a length of 60–70 nt (or shorter), the 5' and 3' splice sites and BPS occupy a large fraction of the intron.
source: At a length of 60–70 nt (or shorter), the 5' and 3' splice sites and BPS occupy a large fraction of the intron.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the known sizes of these sequence elements.

claim: Length-changing mutations may often disrupt recognition of core motifs in 60-70 nt introns, contributing to maintenance of intron length.
source: Thus, length-changing mutations may often disrupt recognition of core motifs in this class, contributing to maintenance of intron length.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that splice site elements occupy a large fraction of these short introns.

claim: Selection for splicing speed and/or accuracy may play a role in maintenance of long introns in genes with particular biological functions, despite the expected mutational pressure toward shortening.
source: Our observation that gene architectures characteristic of exon definition are associated with not only faster but also more accurate splicing prompts us to speculate that selection for splicing speed and/or accuracy may play a role in maintenance of long introns in genes with particular biological functions (discussed below), despite the expected mutational pressure toward shortening.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed relationship between exon definition and splicing speed/accuracy.

claim: The increased time required to transcribe the longer introns characteristic of exon-defined transcripts may afford more time for recognition and proofreading of exon definition complexes on upstream exons.
source: Perhaps, the increased time required to transcribe the longer introns characteristic of exon-defined transcripts affords more time for recognition (and perhaps proofreading) of exon definition complexes on upstream exons.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for why exon definition is associated with faster and more accurate splicing.

claim: Efficient juxtaposition of exons may be favored by tethering of the upstream exon definition complex to the elongating polymerase during transcription of the subsequent exon.
source: It has also been proposed that efficient juxtaposition of exons is favored by tethering of the upstream exon definition complex to the elongating polymerase during transcription of the subsequent exon (Hollander et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism from cited literature.

claim: SR proteins may play a role in accelerating exon definition.
source: Splicing factors of the SR protein family or other families may also play a role in accelerating exon definition, given our observations that particular sequence motifs are enriched in exons associated with exon definition, and previous observations that SR proteins can enhance splicing rates in mammalian systems (Long and Caceres, 2009; Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on observed motif enrichment and cited literature about SR protein function.

claim: Genes with mixed modes of initial splice site recognition had less consistent splicing rates of their introns than genes with predominantly intron or exon definition.
source: We also observed that genes with mixed modes of initial splice site recognition had less consistent splicing rates of their introns than genes with predominantly intron or exon definition.
evidence: This is based on analysis of variance in splicing rates across different gene classes.

claim: If initial pairing of U1 and U2 snRNPs occurs across an intron, the U2 complex bound at the 3' end of the intron might have reduced availability to pair with a U1 snRNP bound to the downstream 5' splice site, inhibiting exon definition downstream.
source: If initial pairing of U1 and U2 snRNPs occurs across an intron, the U2 complex bound at the 3' end of the intron might have reduced availability to pair with a U1 snRNP bound to the downstream 5' splice site, inhibiting exon definition downstream, and conversely (Berget, 1995).
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation supported by citation.

claim: There is a tendency for different introns in the same transcript to use the same mode of initial splice site pairing.
source: Thus, one might expect a tendency for different introns in the same transcript to use the same mode of initial splice site pairing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proposed mechanism of snRNP availability.

claim: There are 5% fewer genes with mixed modes of splicing site recognition than expected by chance (permutation test p<0.001).
source: Indeed, we observe that there are 5% fewer genes with mixed modes of splicing site recognition than expected by chance (permutation test p<0.001).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis comparing observed to expected distributions.

claim: Genes with architectures favoring intron definition were enriched for Gene Ontology categories involved in RNA processing and metabolic processes.
source: We observed that genes with architectures favoring intron definition were enriched for Gene Ontology categories involved in RNA processing and metabolic processes (Supplementary file 2), while genes with predominant exon definition were enriched for developmental processes and stress responses (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on Gene Ontology enrichment analysis.

claim: Genes with predominant exon definition were enriched for developmental processes and stress responses.
source: We observed that genes with architectures favoring intron definition were enriched for Gene Ontology categories involved in RNA processing and metabolic processes (Supplementary file 2), while genes with predominant exon definition were enriched for developmental processes and stress responses (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on Gene Ontology enrichment analysis.

claim: The enrichment within many of the most significant categories of developmental processes and response to oxidative stress increased for genes with increased proportions of exon-defined introns.
source: Furthermore, the enrichment within many of the most significant categories of developmental processes and response to oxidative stress increased for genes with increased proportions of exon-defined introns (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on Gene Ontology enrichment analysis shown in a figure.

claim: Timing of gene expression may be of particular importance during early development, when cell cycles are very short.
source: Timing of gene expression may be of particular importance during early development, when cell cycles are very short (Tadros and Lipshitz, 2009; Artieri and Fraser, 2014), and in stress response when protein production must be turned on quickly.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Timing of gene expression may be of particular importance in stress response when protein production must be turned on quickly.
source: Timing of gene expression may be of particular importance during early development, when cell cycles are very short (Tadros and Lipshitz, 2009; Artieri and Fraser, 2014), and in stress response when protein production must be turned on quickly.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the importance of rapid gene expression in stress response.

claim: Genes in developmental and stress response pathways might have evolved structures that favor exon definition to take advantage of the increased splicing speed and accuracy associated with this mode of recognition.
source: Thus, genes in developmental and stress response pathways might have evolved structures that favor exon definition to take advantage of the increased splicing speed and accuracy associated with this mode of recognition, although rates of other steps (e.g. transcription, 3' end formation) will also contribute to expression dynamics and may be rate limiting in some cases.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed enrichment of exon-defined introns in these gene classes and their faster/more accurate splicing.

claim: The half-life of the last intron is longer than the expected time to transcribe the last exon in 92% of genes expressed in Drosophila S2 cells.
source: Interestingly, the half-life of the last intron is longer than the expected time to transcribe the last exon in 92% of genes expressed in Drosophila S2 cells, making splicing likely to be rate limiting for expression of a large portion of these genes.
evidence: This is based on comparison of measured splicing half-lives to calculated transcription times.

claim: Splicing is likely to be rate limiting for expression of a large portion of genes expressed in Drosophila S2 cells.
source: Interestingly, the half-life of the last intron is longer than the expected time to transcribe the last exon in 92% of genes expressed in Drosophila S2 cells, making splicing likely to be rate limiting for expression of a large portion of these genes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of splicing and transcription times.

claim: Introns in genes with higher expression levels tended to have faster rates of splicing.
source: We also observed that introns in genes with higher expression levels tended to have faster rates of splicing.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the relationship between gene expression and splicing rates.

claim: Genes with higher expression levels have evolved biased codon usage to enhance translation elongation rates and promote efficient ribosome recycling in order to boost the pool of available ribosomes and optimize overall translation efficiency.
source: There is evidence that genes with higher expression levels have evolved biased codon usage to enhance translation elongation rates and promote efficient ribosome recycling in order to boost the pool of available ribosomes and optimize overall translation efficiency (Quax et al., 2015) (Kudla et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Highly expressed genes may have evolved exon definition to boost their speed of splicing and recycling of the splicing machinery in order to boost the pool of free snRNPs and optimize the overall splicing efficiency in the cell.
source: Similarly, highly expressed genes may have evolved exon definition to boost their speed of splicing and recycling of the splicing machinery in order to boost the pool of free snRNPs and optimize the overall splicing efficiency in the cell.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation drawing an analogy to codon usage optimization.
